Goal-directed behavior, such as sustained attention, requires a mechanism for the selective prioritization of contextually appropriate representations.

title: FedNST: Federated Noisy Student Training for Automatic Speech Recognition
text_ai: Federated Learning (FL) enables training state-of-the-art Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) models on user devices (clients) in distributed systems, hence preventing transmission of raw user data to a central server. A key challenge facing practical adoption of FL for ASR is obtaining ground-truth labels on the clients. To overcome this, we propose Federated Noisy Student Training (FedNST), a novel framework that integrates the privacy-preserving advantages of FL with the data-efficiency of Noisy Student Training. FedNST operates by leveraging an iteratively improving global teacher model to generate pseudo-labels for large volumes of local, unlabeled speech data residing on client devices. These pseudo-labels, coupled with data augmentation and noise injection techniques, are then used to train local student models. Only the model updates from these student models are securely aggregated at the central server, ensuring raw audio data never leaves the client. Our extensive experiments on public ASR datasets demonstrate that FedNST significantly enhances model accuracy, particularly in low-resource settings, outperforming traditional FL baselines and achieving competitive results with fully supervised approaches that use substantially more labeled data. This method effectively addresses the labeling scarcity in FL for ASR, enabling robust model training while strictly upholding user data privacy.

title: Tackling solvent effect by coupling electronic and molecular Density Functional Theory
text_ai: Solvation effect might have a tremendous influence on chemical reactions. However, precise quantum chemistry calculations are most often done either in vacuum neglecting the role of the solvent or using continuum solvent model ignoring its molecular nature. To overcome these limitations, we propose a novel hybrid approach that couples electronic Density Functional Theory (DFT) with molecular Density Functional Theory (mDFT). This methodology precisely describes the solute and its immediate solvation shell using electronic DFT, capturing crucial explicit solute-solvent interactions and electronic polarization effects. Concurrently, the bulk solvent environment, including its entropic and structural contributions, is efficiently modeled via mDFT. Such a synergistic coupling allows for a comprehensive treatment of solvent effects, bridging the gap between purely implicit continuum models and computationally expensive fully explicit molecular dynamics simulations. It inherently accounts for the molecular granularity of the solvent while retaining the quantum mechanical accuracy for the reactive core. We demonstrate the efficacy of this coupled eDFT/mDFT framework by applying it to several benchmark systems, including charge transfer reactions and conformational equilibria in aqueous solutions. Our results highlight the method's ability to accurately predict reaction free energies, pKa values, and spectroscopic shifts, which are often poorly reproduced by conventional methods. This approach offers a robust and computationally tractable strategy for a more accurate and nuanced understanding of chemical processes in condensed phases, paving the way for predictive simulations of complex solution-phase chemistry.

title: Economic Rationality under Specialization: Evidence of Decision Bias in AI Agents
text_ai: In the study by Chen et al. (2023) [01], the large language model GPT demonstrated economic rationality comparable to or exceeding the average human level in tasks such as budget allocation and risk preference. This paper investigates whether domain specialization, while enhancing performance in specific economic functions, inadvertently introduces systematic decision biases in AI agents. We developed and tested AI agents optimized for distinct economic roles in a simulated market, assessing their performance in complex, inter-domain decision scenarios. Our findings reveal that despite specialized proficiency, these agents consistently exhibit biases—such as anchoring and confirmation bias—when decisions extend beyond their immediate scope, leading to sub-optimal systemic economic outcomes. These results underscore the critical need to design AI systems that mitigate emergent biases in specialized architectures for complex economic applications.

title: DIViS: Domain Invariant Visual Servoing for Collision-Free Goal Reaching
text_ai: Robots should understand both semantics and physics to be functional in the real world. While robot platforms provide means for interacting with the physical world they cannot autonomously acquire object-level semantics without needing human. In this paper, we investigate how to minimize human effort and intervention to teach robots perform real world tasks that incorporate semantics. This paper introduces DIViS, a novel framework for **Domain Invariant Visual Servoing** enabling robots to autonomously execute semantic goal-reaching tasks with minimal human intervention. Our core contribution is a self-supervised learning strategy extracting **domain-invariant visual features**, robustly encoding semantics across diverse environments without extensive re-training. These semantic features are integrated into a reactive **visual servoing** control loop, guiding the robot directly towards desired semantic targets. Crucially, DIViS incorporates an inherent **collision-free** navigation capability, dynamically planning safe paths in the feature space by maintaining distances from detected obstacles in novel, cluttered environments. We demonstrate DIViS's efficacy on a physical robot platform across various real-world scenarios, showcasing superior performance in **collision-free goal reaching**, robustness to domain shifts, and reduced human effort compared to state-of-the-art methods.

title: Significant core shift variability in parsec-scale jets of active galactic nuclei
text_ai: The apparent position of jet base (core) in radio-loud active galactic nuclei changes with frequency because of synchrotron self-absorption. Studying this `core shift` effect enables us to reconstruct properties of the jet regions close to the central engine. While core shift has conventionally been treated as a relatively stable characteristic, its temporal variability, reflecting dynamic changes in the jet's physical conditions, has remained largely unexplored. Understanding this variability is crucial for accurately interpreting single-epoch measurements and for advancing models of jet launching and collimation. This paper presents a comprehensive multi-epoch, multi-frequency Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI) investigation into core shift in a sample of prominent active galactic nuclei. By meticulously monitoring the frequency-dependent core positions over several years, we reveal significant and often rapid variations in both the magnitude and direction of the core shift parameter. These observed variations frequently exceed typical measurement uncertainties, strongly indicating intrinsic changes within the parsec-scale jet. We explore potential correlations between core shift variability and other observable parameters, such as flux density outbursts and spectral index changes, to identify the underlying physical mechanisms. Our findings challenge static jet models and underscore the highly dynamic nature of the inner jet regions. The observed core shift variability provides critical observational constraints for time-dependent models of jet emission and propagation, emphasizing the need to account for transient phenomena when deriving fundamental jet parameters like magnetic field strength and particle density profiles. This work highlights that core shift is a dynamic probe of the evolving physical environment near the supermassive black hole.

title: Measurement of the Higgs boson mass with $H \rightarrow \gamma\gamma$ decays in 140 fb$^{-1}$ of $\sqrt{s}=13$ TeV $pp$ collisions with the ATLAS detector
text_ai: The mass of the Higgs boson is measured in the $H\to\gamma\gamma$ decay channel, exploiting the high resolution of the invariant mass of photon pairs reconstructed from the decays of Higgs bosons produced in proton-proton collisions at a centre-of-mass energy $\sqrt{s}=13$ TeV. This analysis uses the full 140 fb$^{-1}$ ATLAS Run 2 dataset. A binned maximum-likelihood fit to the diphoton invariant mass spectrum extracts the Higgs boson mass, employing a Crystal Ball function for the signal and an empirical function for the background. Systematic uncertainties, notably from photon energy scale and resolution and background modeling, are carefully evaluated. The measured Higgs boson mass is determined to be $m_H = 125.XX \pm Y_{stat} \text{(stat)} \pm Z_{syst} \text{(syst)}$ GeV. This represents the most precise measurement in the $H \rightarrow \gamma\gamma$ channel by ATLAS to date, consistent with Standard Model predictions.
